sentences.gloss_en: Welcome to today's explainer.
Together we're going on a fun visual journey, unpacking the natural evolution of data.
That is, how we move from weak, error-filled spreadsheets to strong, orderly databases.
This journey isn't just an infographic; it's a complete rethink of how we build our database foundations correctly from the very start.
OK, let's get straight into it and look at our roadmap.
Number 1: moving from spreadsheets to databases; number 2: data constraints and normalization; number 3: the SQL command families.
Number 4: the query execution funnel; number 5: the grain and LIMIT 1; and finally number 6: the worlds of NoSQL. Let's go!
Number 1: from spreadsheets to databases, and how we end the chaos of files.
Why do we say these flat CSV files cause chaos?
Imagine several people trying to edit the same file at the same time.
The result: whoever saves last wipes out everyone else's work — literally a disaster.
On top of that, to find just one row the computer has to read the whole file from start to end.
Worse still, there's no protection stopping someone from entering nonsense where numbers belong, or the reverse.
And here's where the magic happens: we watch this grid turn into a real database table.
The database gives us a very strong structure.
First: a date column, for example, whose type is DATE can never accept a word like 'maybe'.
Second: this gives each row a single unique identity.
Third: what builds the relationships, whether one-to-many or many-to-many, using junction tables like order_items.
Number 2: data constraints and normalization.
These constraints aren't just decoration.
They're like solid walls protecting our database, rejecting any bad data with clear reasons because they represent the business rules.
NOT NULL says, with total strictness, there are no empty cells here.
UNIQUE guarantees there's no duplicated identity.
CHECK enforces logic, like the amount can never be negative.
And the foreign key stops us pointing at ghosts — we can never link data to something that doesn't exist.
Now it's time for our first prediction question.
Four rows are trying to get into the database; which one do you think will hit the wall and be rejected?
Look closely and we find this orphan row, order 1007, pointing at customer 9.
In reality we have no customer number 9 in the customers table, so the foreign key rejects it immediately.
As for normalization, the idea is simply like cutting a wide, repetition-filled table into smaller, smarter tables.
In 1NF we make values atomic; in 2NF we ensure dependence on the whole key; and in 3NF we prevent transitive dependence.
All this is to prevent update anomalies.
But note: in analytics we sometimes do the opposite and resort to denormalization to speed up dashboards and reduce joins.
Number 3: SQL command families — the commands are divided into five families.
DDL to define tables, DML to modify data, DQL to query, DCL for permissions, and TCL for transactions.
There are very common mistakes here, like writing SELECT * in production, because it pulls resources for nothing.
And comparing a value with = NULL instead of IS NULL.
The key point is UNION: it runs a check to remove duplicates, and that slows performance a lot.
So if we're sure the data is unique, always use UNION ALL because it's much faster.
Number 4: the query execution funnel — the most important part of our journey: how does the engine really think?
The surprise: the database engine doesn't read the code top to bottom the way we write it.
This strip shows the nine stages in the logical order of execution.
It starts with FROM, then JOIN, then WHERE — the cheapest and biggest performance win, because any row filtered here never reaches the heavy operations after it.
Then GROUP BY, then HAVING; only now does SELECT run; then DISTINCT, then ORDER BY; and the very last thing executed is LIMIT.
Let's build this funnel with numbers to see how it works in practice.
We started with 14 rows; as soon as the JOIN ran, the count dropped to 13.
Why? Because the JOIN quietly removed the orphan row, order 1007, simply because it can't find its customer.
Then the WHERE stage kicks in: this filter dropped cancelled order 1004 and refunded order 1010.
So the funnel took us from 13 rows down to just 11.
When we reach GROUP BY, those 11 rows are compressed hard into just 2 groups: the gold tier and the silver tier.
See how the funnel works? It started at 14, then 13, dropped to 11, until it reached 2.
This result confirms our work and our aggregation are exactly right.
If we add gold sales of 3098.30 euros to silver sales of 850.20 euros, we get a total of 3948.5 euros.
This number proves our data pipeline is 100% sound from start to finish, with no data lost along the way.
And this brings us to the most famous error in all of SQL.
Why does the code fail if we write WHERE revenue greater than 300?
The secret is in the funnel: the alias named revenue is born at the sixth stage, at SELECT.
But WHERE runs very early, at the third stage, so WHERE has never even heard of anything called revenue.
The right fix here is to use HAVING SUM, or to use a CTE.
Number 5: the grain and LIMIT 1.
Here we come to our second prediction question, one that confuses heavyweights with experience in the field.
If we put LIMIT 1 at the end of the query, does the engine really save effort and computation under the hood? Yes or no?
The surprise? Of course not: the engine still has to compute and sort all the groups fully to know which winner comes first.
All LIMIT does is reduce the amount of data sent over the network; it doesn't save any computation.
So our funnel ends at 1, but only after all the heavy work has been done.
Now the million-dollar question before writing any line of code: what is the grain? What exactly does one row represent?
Is it an order? A customer? A customer-day?
If we compute the SUM on the wrong grain, the dashboard shows a very confident-looking number that is unfortunately completely wrong and doesn't reflect reality.
Strict relational tables aren't always the magic solution for everything.
In the amazing worlds of NoSQL we have other solutions that suit different needs.
Document stores like MongoDB, great at nested schemas.
Key-value like Redis, the caching champion with its blazing speed, with a TTL of 3600.
Wide-column like Cassandra, designed around the query, with a replication factor of 3.
And finally graph databases like Neo4j, brilliant at tracing relationships and shortest paths.
That brings us to our design's final outputs: the ERD diagram, a DDL file, and 6 queries, each clearly labeled with its grain.
Our closing question after all this: are you ready to build your data architecture with real awareness?
And will you know the grain of every row before you write your next query?
We hope this journey shed light on many important points. Thank you.
